st.t: Coding copilots: Completion speed excludes checking costs
st.an: CUPS accepts the distinction between completion speed and the human work surrounding AI suggestions, and materially develops it by quantifying Copilot-specific interaction states, showing that checking can continue after acceptance, and proposing better verification and code-retention metrics. Because it has no unaided baseline, it complements rather than challenges the randomized completion-time finding.

st.t: Coding workflow: Generation overhead limits productivity gains
st.an: The CUPS study accepts the cluster’s core view that productivity depends on the surrounding human workflow and materially strengthens it with a participant-labeled taxonomy and richer measurement of verification, editing and prompting overhead. It finds that conventional metrics substantially undercount interaction time while carefully avoiding the stronger claim that Copilot causes a net productivity loss.

Moreover, we show that such analysis nearly doubles our estimates for how much developer time can be attributed to interactions with code suggestion systems, as compared with existing metrics.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source extends the cluster’s proposition with a concrete state-level framework for measuring hidden human work in AI-assisted workflows. Its narrow, artificial task setting limits generalisation to legal practice.

st.an: The source supports the cluster’s caution against inferring productivity from perceived usefulness or preference. Its review of conflicting coding experiments reinforces the cluster’s emphasis on objective measurement and task-specific effects, though it does not address durable skill formation directly or contribute new productivity evidence.

st.an: The source supports the cluster’s cautious distinction between observing AI-assisted workflows and demonstrating productivity gains. Its interaction-focused protocol can identify user costs and behavior, but the deliberate absence of an unaided baseline means it cannot estimate whether Copilot saves or consumes time relative to human-only work.

kp.k: CUPS profiles AI-assisted programming beyond acceptance telemetry
kp.d: Mozannar, Bansal, Fourney and Horvitz introduce CodeRec User Programming States (CUPS), a taxonomy of 12 programmer activities that combines retrospective participant labels with interaction telemetry. Its purpose is to identify human intentions, verification work, prompting and other interaction costs that acceptance rates, tokens saved and overall completion times do not adequately capture. This is programming-domain evidence, not a study of legal work.
qs: The leaf nodes of the finalized taxonomy represent 12 distinct states that programmers can find themselves in.
Prior interaction metrics also largely miss user effort invested in devising and refining prompts used to query the models.

kp.k: Study measures interaction, not causal productivity gains
kp.d: The study recruited 21 participants within the authors' organization, assigned familiar tasks from eight preselected tasks, and collected 3137 CUPS labels through immediate retrospective annotation. Nineteen participants used Python, one C++ and one JavaScript; 11 had never used Copilot. Mean session duration was 12.23 minutes. The system studied was Copilot as of August 2022. Section 5.2 reports 1024 displayed suggestions and 34.0% accepted, whereas the introduction reports interaction with 1096 suggestions. There was no unassisted comparison condition.
qs: The version of Copilot that this manuscript refers to is Copilot as of August 2022.
During the coding tasks, Copilot showed participants a total of 1024 suggestions, out of which they accepted 34.0%.

We do not include a baseline condition where participants perform the coding task without Copilot, as this work focuses on understanding and modeling the interaction with the current version of Copilot.

kp.k: Verification and editing consume substantial session time
kp.d: Averaged across participants, verifying suggestions occupied 22.4% of session time, writing new functionality 14.05%, editing the last suggestion 11.90%, prompt crafting 11.56%, and waiting for suggestions 4.2%. The conclusion reports 34.3% for double-checking and editing combined. Copilot-specific states together occupied 51.5% of average session duration, with sample standard deviation 19.3. These are allocations within assisted sessions, not estimates of net additional time relative to unaided programming.
qs: We found that the total time participants spend in these states is 51.5 % (sN = 19.3) of the average session duration.
all participants spend more than 21% of their time in these states.
may spend a large fraction of total session time (34.3%) on just double-checking and editing Copilot suggestions

kp.k: Acceptance can precede substantive human verification
kp.d: The authors counted 61 states in which programmers deferred thought about suggestions. Users could accept code to obtain syntax highlighting or to assemble successive fragments before checking their combined meaning. Accepted suggestions were edited with probability 0.53 when verification had been deferred, compared with 0.18 when verified beforehand; the authors report this difference as statistically significant. Suggestion character count and line count did not statistically distinguish deferred from previously verified suggestions.
qs: This occurs either because programmers wish to see the suggestion with code highlighting, or because they want to see where Copilot suggestions leads to.
However, when we look at the likelihood of editing an accepted suggestion, we find that it is 0.18 if it was verified before, but it is 0.53 if it was deferred.

kp.k: Post-acceptance checking changes measured verification costs
kp.d: For accepted suggestions with deferred thought, programmers verified immediately afterward 53.2% of the time. Accounting for post-acceptance checking raised mean measured time from 3.25 to 15.21 seconds and median time from 1.99 to 6.48 seconds. Even when suggestions had been checked before acceptance, 19% received subsequent verification, increasing mean verification time from 3.96 to 7.03 seconds. The authors recommend including post-acceptance verification and tracking whether accepted suggestions remain in the codebase.
qs: First, when participants defer their thought about a suggestion they accepted, 53.2% of the time they verify the suggestion immediately afterward.
We recommend using measures such as the fraction of suggestions accepted that survive in the codebase after a certain time period (e.g. 10 minutes).

kp.k: Prompt crafting creates iterative work and possible interruptions
kp.d: Only 10.7% of 234 suggestions displayed while participants were actively prompt crafting were accepted. The authors hypothesize that users preferred to formulate prompts themselves and interpret these suggestions as unnecessary interruptions. Across 59 prompt-crafting attempts, 81.3% included an accepted suggestion. Participants prompted through comments, docstrings and function signatures or variable names, often combining approaches and revising prompts after inspecting output.
qs: Among 234 suggestions that were shown while participants were actively prompt crafting, defined as a suggestion where a programmer was prompt crafting while the suggestion was being displayed, only 10.7% were accepted.
Often, programmers combine the three prompt crafting strategies to get better code suggestions.

kp.d: The state-machine analysis found transitions from writing new functionality to verification with probability 0.59, prompt crafting to verification with probability 0.54, and prompt crafting to waiting with probability 0.25. The authors propose grouping successive suggestions when users defer verification, prioritizing resources when users wait, and suppressing suggestions during prompt composition. These are proposed interventions, not demonstrated improvements; reliable automated state prediction remains future work.
qs: If the programmer is observed to have been deferring their thought on the last few         suggestions, group successive Copilot suggestions and display them together.
However, the current amount of labeled data is not sufficient to build highly accurate models.

kp.k: Perceived productivity benefits coexist with quality concerns
kp.d: In the post-study survey, 17 of 21 participants agreed that Copilot helped them complete the task faster, and 16 of 21 agreed that they were more productive. Fourteen of 21 agreed that it helped them stay in flow and spend less time searching for information; six expressed concern about code quality. These are participant perceptions rather than experimentally established productivity or quality effects. Differences by programming expertise and prior Copilot use were considered insufficient to establish their influence on behavior.
qs: Finally, 17/21 participants agreed with the statement that by using Copilot, they completed the task faster, and 16/21 participants agreed that they were more productive using Copilot.
Due to the limited number of participants, these results are not sufficient to determine the influence of programmer experience or Copilot experience on behavior.

kp.k: Short tasks leave longer-term costs unresolved
kp.d: The authors qualify their findings because participants performed selected, time-limited tasks rather than their own real-world work, predominantly in Python. Annotation assigned one state per telemetry segment even though multiple activities could occur; IDK segments representing 6.5% of total session time were excluded. Security vulnerabilities, overreliance and longer-horizon consequences were not assessed. Time is explicitly treated as an incomplete proxy for multidimensional interaction costs.
qs: First, our participants solved time-limited coding tasks that were provided by us instead of real tasks they may perform in the real world.
We also did not capture longer-term costs of interacting, e.g., from accepting code with security vulnerabilities or longer horizon costs.
We use time as a proxy to study the new costs of interaction introduced by the AI system.

kp.k: Legal applications are proposed methodological extensions
kp.d: The authors explicitly suggest developing analogous taxonomies for writing assistants used by creative writers or lawyers. They also propose counterfactual studies comparing assisted and unassisted workflows to determine where checking and editing costs are outweighed by avoided manual effort. The document supplies a framework for investigating legal-AI interaction, but no empirical findings about lawyers, law-firm structures, legal pricing or regulation.
qs: For example, one can make an analogous CUPS taxonomy for writing assistants for creative writers or lawyers.
One option is to conduct a new study where we compare the CUPS diagram with Copilot assistance with a counterfactual condition where the programmers don’t have access to Copilot.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Mozannar, Bansal, Fourney and Horvitz find that Copilot changes programming workflows by introducing substantial verification, editing, prompting and waiting work.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain study of AI-assisted programming, not an empirical study of legal services. The authors report that verification occupies 22.4% of the average session, editing the last suggestion 11.9%, and the five Copilot-specific activity states together 51.5%. These are allocations of observed session time, not estimates of net additional time relative to programming without AI.

pts.k: Accepting AI-generated code does not necessarily mean that the programmer has verified it; conventional acceptance and timing metrics miss subsequent work.
pts.d: The authors observe that users sometimes accept code to obtain syntax highlighting or to assemble multiple suggestions before checking them. Including subsequent verification raises mean attributed time for deferred suggestions from 3.25 to 15.21 seconds. Even suggestions checked before acceptance sometimes receive further checking, raising the reported mean from 3.96 to 7.03 seconds. Deferred suggestions are more likely to be edited than previously verified suggestions. The authors recommend measuring whether accepted code survives over time rather than treating acceptance alone as utility.

pts.k: Prompting is iterative, and suggestions delivered while users are crafting prompts are often ignored.
pts.d: The authors report that only 10.7% of 234 suggestions displayed during active prompt crafting were accepted. They identify 59 prompt-crafting attempts, 81.3% of which included acceptance of a suggestion. They hypothesize that programmers prefer composing prompts themselves and interpret suggestions during prompt composition as unnecessary interruptions; that explanation is an interpretation rather than a tested causal finding.

pts.k: Participants generally perceived productivity and flow benefits despite the interaction costs.
pts.d: The authors report that 17 of 21 participants felt they completed the task faster, 16 of 21 felt more productive, and 14 of 21 agreed with statements about maintaining flow and spending less time searching for information. Six expressed code-quality concerns. These are participant perceptions, not controlled measurements of productivity gains in this study.

pts.k: State-aware interfaces could reduce interaction inefficiencies, but these improvements remain proposals.
pts.d: The authors propose grouping successive suggestions when users defer verification, prioritizing resources when users wait, and suppressing suggestions during prompt composition. Implementation would require users to signal their state or sufficiently accurate real-time state prediction. The authors also suggest adapting their methodology to writing assistants for lawyers; they do not claim demonstrated legal-sector benefits.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is a mixed-methods study combining telemetry, retrospective participant labeling and a post-study survey.
pts.d: Twenty-one programmers from one large organization performed assigned coding tasks and immediately labeled recordings using the 12-state CUPS taxonomy. The analysis includes 3,137 CUPS labels; 353 uncertain labels, representing 6.5% of session time, were excluded. Section 5.2 reports 1,024 displayed suggestions, whereas the introduction reports interactions with 1,096 suggestions. The paper uses descriptive statistics, transition probabilities and significance tests for selected comparisons. It has no no-Copilot baseline. Related-work productivity results are attributed to other studies and are not findings from this experiment.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern the August 2022 version of Copilot used in short experimental sessions, not long-term deployment or later systems.
pts.d: The supplied manuscript is the April 2024 arXiv version. Tasks were selected to fit approximately 20 minutes, with a mean session duration of 12.23 minutes; 19 of 21 participants used Python. Participants performed researcher-provided tasks rather than their ordinary work. Each telemetry segment received only one activity label, potentially collapsing multiple activities. Long-term maintenance, security vulnerabilities and overreliance were not assessed. The authors regard experience-group comparisons as inconclusive because of sample size and leave net productivity assessment to future counterfactual studies.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are programmers using code-recommendation assistants and developers designing or measuring those assistants.
pts.d: The participant pool comprised software engineers of varying seniority, researchers and graduate student interns, including both experienced Copilot users and first-time users. Programmers perform human verification, editing and prompting while potentially benefiting from reduced manual coding and information search. Tool designers and evaluators are encouraged to measure these activities and adapt interfaces to user needs. This is human-in-the-loop assistance, not evidence of autonomous programmer replacement. Lawyers appear only as a prospective population for analogous methodology; the paper makes no findings about law-firm staffing, legal pricing, legal markets or access to justice.
